topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Consumer group membership
description: All KafkaConsumer instances that share the same group.id belong to one consumer group. Kafka's broker-side group coordination automatically balances the partitions of subscribed topics among the live members of the group, so a group functions as a single logical subscriber even though it is made of many processes. This is the mechanism that lets consumption scale horizontally: adding more consumer processes to the same group.id increases parallelism without any application-level coordination code.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Consumer position as a single integer offset
description: The Kafka design documentation states: 'the position of a consumer in each partition is just a single integer, the offset of the next message to consume.' This is a deliberate departure from traditional message queues (e.g. JMS brokers), which must track per-message acknowledgment state for every consumer. Because position is one number per partition, it is cheap to store, cheap to advance, and cheap to rewind: a consumer can deliberately seek backward to an earlier offset to reprocess data, which most point-to-point queueing systems do not support.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once
description: Per the official design documentation: at-most-once means messages may be lost but are never redelivered, achieved by committing offsets before processing completes. At-least-once means messages are never lost but may be redelivered -- this is the default behavior when offsets are committed after processing. Exactly-once means each message is processed exactly once; the docs state this requires 'coordinating the consumer's position with what is actually stored as output,' which in practice means using a transactional producer together with a read_committed consumer. These are not consumer-only settings -- the achieved semantic is a joint property of producer config (acks, idempotence, transactions) and consumer config (commit timing, isolation.level).

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Partition-to-consumer exclusivity
description: The javadoc states the assignment invariant directly: 'if there is a topic with four partitions, and a consumer group with two processes, each process would consume from two partitions.' This exclusivity is what gives Kafka in-order, non-duplicated delivery per partition within a group -- two members of the same group never read the same partition concurrently. It also caps useful parallelism: a group cannot usefully have more active consumers than the topic has partitions, because the excess consumers will be assigned zero partitions.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: auto.offset.reset governs behavior when no valid committed offset exists
description: Documented as controlling 'what to do when there is no initial offset in Kafka or if the current offset does not exist any more on the server,' with a default of latest. A brand-new consumer group, or a group whose committed offset has aged out of the topic's retention window, hits this fallback. 'latest' starts consumption from the newest record, silently skipping any backlog -- appropriate for consumers that only care about new events. 'earliest' starts from the oldest retained record, reprocessing the full available history -- appropriate when completeness matters more than avoiding reprocessing. This setting only applies in the absence of a usable committed offset; it does not override an existing valid commit. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Cited page https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/consumer-configs/ documents FOUR values for auto.offset.reset (earliest, latest, by_duration:<duration>, none); the row presents only two. 'none' (throw if no committed offset) is the fail-loud option and the direct remedy for the K-041 trap. Incomplete against its own source at operation depth. Default 'latest' is confirmed correct.]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: commitSync vs commitAsync
description: When manual commit is chosen, KafkaConsumer exposes commitSync(), which blocks the calling thread until the commit either succeeds or fails, and commitAsync(), which returns immediately and optionally invokes a callback. The javadoc frames manual control as necessary whenever 'the consumption of the messages is coupled with some processing logic and hence a message should not be considered as consumed until it is completed processing' -- i.e. whenever correctness requires the commit to happen only after work is done, not on a timer. It also states the convention that 'the committed offset should always be the offset of the next message that your application will read,' not the offset of the last message read.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: ConsumerRebalanceListener callbacks
description: The javadoc describes ConsumerRebalanceListener as the hook for application-level logic around rebalances. onPartitionsRevoked(Collection) is called when partitions are about to be taken from the consumer, giving the application a chance to 'finish necessary application-level logic such as state cleanup, manual offset commits' before losing ownership. onPartitionsAssigned(Collection) is called after new partitions are assigned, letting the consumer call seek() to initialize its read position for those partitions if it needs something other than the last committed offset. Without registering this listener, applications cannot reliably commit in-flight work before a partition moves to another consumer.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: enable.idempotence config and its enforced constraints
description: enable.idempotence is documented as: 'when set to true, the producer will ensure that exactly one copy of each message is written in the stream.' Kafka does not let this be enabled in isolation -- it enforces (or auto-corrects) three other settings: max.in.flight.requests.per.connection must be at most 5 (idempotence needs the broker to see requests in an order it can validate sequence numbers against, which breaks down with unbounded in-flight requests), retries must be greater than 0 (idempotence exists specifically to make retries safe, so disabling retries defeats its purpose), and acks must be 'all' (idempotence's guarantee is only meaningful if the broker's ack reflects full replication). Since Kafka 3.0, enable.idempotence defaults to true, meaning these constraints are the default behavior unless a user explicitly reconfigures around them.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: group.instance.id config field
description: The consumer-configs reference documents group.instance.id tersely: 'a unique identifier of the consumer instance provided by the end user,' defaulting to null (i.e. dynamic/ephemeral membership, the ordinary mode). This is the literal config surface behind the static-membership behavior described in KIP-345 (separate row): the KIP explains why the feature exists and what it trades off, this entry documents the exact knob that turns it on. Operators must supply a value that is unique per physical consumer instance within the group -- collisions produce FENCED_INSTANCE_ID errors rather than silent misbehavior. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Row claims canon 'documents group.instance.id tersely' as only 'a unique identifier of the consumer instance provided by the end user' and builds a claim on that truncation. The cited 4.3 page continues: 'If set, the consumer is treated as a static member, which means that only one instance with this ID is allowed in the consumer group at any time. This can be used in combination with a larger session timeout to avoid group rebalances caused by transient unavailability.' The row's assertion ABOUT ITS OWN SOURCE is false -- a first-sentence-only read.]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: group.protocol config selects classic vs next-generation rebalancing
description: group.protocol is documented as 'the group protocol that the consumer uses,' defaulting to classic. Setting it to consumer opts the client into the KIP-848 protocol. Per the consumer-rebalance-protocol operations page, migration supports both offline and online (rolling) upgrade paths, and once a consumer runs the new protocol, legacy configs like heartbeat.interval.ms, session.timeout.ms, and partition.assignment.strategy become unavailable on that client -- the equivalent broker-side group.consumer.* settings govern those values instead. Known limitations at time of writing: client-side custom assignors are unsupported, and rack-aware assignment strategies are not yet fully supported under the new protocol.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: isolation.level: read_committed vs read_uncommitted, and offset gaps from control messages
description: The javadoc states that in read_committed mode 'the consumer will read only those transactional messages which have been successfully committed. It will continue to read non-transactional messages as before.' Internally this works via the Last Stable Offset (LSO): a read_committed consumer will not deliver messages past the LSO until it knows their transaction's outcome. The javadoc warns of a specific, easy-to-misdiagnose behavior: 'partitions with transactional messages will include commit or abort markers... applications reading from topics with transactional messages will see gaps in the consumed offsets' -- so code that assumes consecutive offsets (e.g. to detect missing messages) will misfire on any topic that uses transactions, even without message loss. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Summary states read_committed makes the consumer 'buffer and skip' aborted-transaction messages. The cited javadoc says verbatim: 'There is no client-side buffering in read_committed mode.' Summary also attributes marker-induced offset gaps to read_committed, where the javadoc says markers 'are filtered out for consumers in both isolation levels.' The row's own description is accurate; only the summary is wrong.]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe
description: The javadoc states plainly: 'The Kafka consumer is NOT thread-safe. It is the responsibility of the user to ensure that multi-threaded access is properly synchronized. Un-synchronized access will result in ConcurrentModificationException.' The single documented exception is wakeup(), which 'can safely be used from an external thread to interrupt an active operation,' causing the blocked call to throw WakeupException so the consumer can shut down cleanly. This constraint is why the decoupled-processing pattern (separate row) requires care: the worker threads must never call consumer methods directly.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Manual partition assignment bypasses group coordination
description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc documents assign() as an alternate, lower-level API: it 'disables dynamic partition assignment and consumer group coordination.' A consumer using assign() specifies its partitions directly and does not participate in rebalances, heartbeats, or the group protocol at all -- it is not a member of a consumer group in the coordination sense even if group.id is set. This matters operationally because none of the rebalance-related configuration (session.timeout.ms, ConsumerRebalanceListener, static membership, cooperative assignors) applies to assign()-based consumers.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: partition.assignment.strategy default list
description: partition.assignment.strategy is documented as 'a list of class names or class types...of supported partition assignment strategies,' with the current default value being the pair RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor. Because it is a list, the client and every other group member negotiate down to the first strategy in the list that all members mutually support; this is how a fleet can be rolled from one assignor to another (e.g. migrating toward cooperative rebalancing per KIP-429) without a hard cutover -- during the transition window, members advertise both and the group converges on whichever both the old and new members share.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Rebalance triggers
description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc lists the conditions that cause the group coordinator to trigger a rebalance: a new consumer joining the group, an existing consumer leaving (gracefully or by crash/timeout), and topic metadata changes such as new partitions being added to a subscribed topic. Each of these events changes group membership or the set of resources to divide, so the coordinator must recompute and redistribute partition ownership across the current members.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: session.timeout.ms and heartbeat.interval.ms
description: session.timeout.ms is described as 'the timeout used to detect client failures when using Kafka's group management facility' -- if no heartbeat arrives within this window, the coordinator triggers a rebalance and gives the dead consumer's partitions to other members. heartbeat.interval.ms controls the frequency of the background heartbeat thread's pings to the coordinator. These two settings are broker-side-configurable defaults too (group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms / group.consumer.session.timeout.ms) with the same numeric defaults (5000ms / 45000ms) in the newer consumer group protocol. Lowering session.timeout.ms detects real failures faster but increases the odds of false-positive rebalances from transient GC pauses or network blips.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: transaction.timeout.ms bounds how long an open transaction can block consumers
description: Documented as 'the maximum amount of time in milliseconds that a transaction will remain open before the coordinator proactively aborts it,' with a default of 60000ms. This setting is not just a producer-side cleanup knob: because read_committed consumers buffer transactional messages until they see the transaction's outcome marker, an abnormally long-lived open transaction directly stalls downstream consumption. transaction.timeout.ms is the backstop that guarantees a hung or crashed transactional producer cannot block read_committed consumers indefinitely.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Auto-commit timing window
description: A widely repeated mistake is assuming auto-commit means 'Kafka safely tracks my progress for me.' In practice, the automatic commit fires on the next call to poll() and commits the offsets returned by the previous poll() -- it is decoupled from whether the consumer actually finished processing those records. If the consumer crashes after poll() returns a batch but before it finishes handling all records in that batch, the next commit (on the following poll or the commit interval, default 5s via auto.commit.interval.ms) may commit offsets past records that were never fully processed, silently dropping them from the at-least-once guarantee people assume auto-commit provides. A related, separately documented race: calling pause() during graceful shutdown while auto-commit is on can seek to stale cached offsets and overwrite correct committed offsets, causing already-processed messages to be reprocessed on restart. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://github.com/confluentinc/confluent-kafka-javascript/issues/404 is a client-library bug report: pause() seeks to a stale #lastConsumedOffsets entry and commits it immediately under enable.auto.commit=true. That is not the general 'auto-commit commits the offset from the last poll(), not the batch just processed' mechanism the row asserts. Related phenomenon, wrong mechanism. Repoint origin to the KafkaConsumer javadoc, which does support the claim.]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: max.poll.interval.ms and CommitFailedException
description: A very common production error is 'Commit cannot be completed since the group has already rebalanced and assigned the partitions to another member' (CommitFailedException). The instinctive read is a broker or network problem; the actual cause documented across support threads and blog postmortems is that the time between successive poll() calls exceeded max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes), because record processing inside the poll loop took too long. The coordinator has no other signal that a consumer is alive except calls to poll(), so it evicts the member and reassigns its partitions, and the pending commit is then rejected as coming from a member no longer in the group. The two accepted fixes are raising max.poll.interval.ms to match real processing time, or lowering max.poll.records so each batch finishes well inside the interval -- one case study reported an 80% drop in rebalances after cutting max.poll.records from 500 to 50.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Poison pill messages block the whole partition
description: When a consumer's deserializer cannot parse a record (commonly because a producer changed serialization format, or the consumer is configured with the wrong key/value deserializer), the default behavior is that the exception is thrown before the offset for that record is ever advanced. Because the consumer re-polls and hits the same record again, it enters an infinite retry loop against that one 'poison pill' message, and every other message queued behind it on that partition is starved indefinitely -- this is not a whole-consumer crash, it is a silent partition-level stall that can go unnoticed until lag alarms fire. Confluent's own guidance is to never let deserialization exceptions propagate up to block re-polling; the documented fix (for the Java/Spring stack) is a wrapping ErrorHandlingDeserializer that catches the failure, returns null plus a DeserializationException header, and routes the record to a dead-letter topic via a recoverer, which lets the offset advance past the bad record.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: read_committed does not mean 'only transactional records'
description: isolation.level controls how a consumer treats transactional writes: read_uncommitted (the default) returns every record including ones from transactions that later abort, while read_committed withholds records from a transaction until it commits (using the Last Stable Offset as the visibility boundary) and drops records from aborted transactions entirely. The trap is assuming read_committed changes what non-transactional writes are visible -- it does not; ordinary produce calls outside any transaction are always visible immediately regardless of isolation.level. This matters for the exactly-once contract: a consumer must explicitly set isolation.level=read_committed to get end-to-end transactional semantics, since the client default is read_uncommitted, so a pipeline that enables producer transactions but forgets to set the consumer's isolation level will still see uncommitted/aborted data.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Rebalances are stop-the-world for the whole group, not just the changed member
description: Under the classic eager rebalance protocol, when group membership changes -- a new consumer joins, one leaves, one is evicted for missing max.poll.interval.ms, or partition count changes -- ALL consumers in the group temporarily pause processing, commit their current offsets, and revoke ownership of every partition they held, before partitions are reassigned. This is not scoped to the consumer that changed: even a member consuming an entirely unrelated set of partitions pauses. In environments with frequent restarts (rolling deploys, transient network blips, autoscaling), this compounds into 'rebalance storms' where overlapping restarts chain into repeated full-group pauses, and one case study found a rolling restart of 5 consumers triggering 10 separate rebalances. The documented mitigations are static group membership (group.instance.id) so brief restarts don't drop a member from the group at all, and the CooperativeStickyAssignor (default assignor pairing since Kafka 2.4+/3.0), which reassigns only the specific partitions that must move instead of revoking everything.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Confluent Apache Kafka 101 -- Hands-on Exercise: Kafka Consumer
description: Part of Confluent's free Apache Kafka 101 course. The reader signs up for a Confluent Cloud cluster, sets up a Python virtual environment and the confluent-kafka client library, configures real connection credentials, and writes a working consumer script with group.id=python_kafka101_group_1 and auto.offset.reset=earliest so it reads from the start of a topic with no committed offsets. The consumer polls in a loop and handles graceful disconnection. Confirmed live and working when fetched: it is a concrete, executable exercise (not just narrative documentation), and it exercises consumer groups, offset management, and partition assignment through the group mechanism.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics

The reader builds consumer.py with group.id='hello_group', auto.offset.reset='earliest', and enable.auto.commit=False, implements an assignment_callback() to observe partition assignment, polls with consumer.poll(1.0), and manually commits offsets with consumer.commit(event) after processing. The exercise then has the reader add and remove consumer instances from the group to observe live rebalancing behavior. Confirmed live and working when fetched, with concrete code and steps.

The reader provisions a Confluent Cloud cluster with Java client credentials, examines a transactional producer that initializes a transactional.id, sends 5 events under one transaction, and either commits or times it out. The core exercise: run a console consumer with isolation.level=read_committed and observe that it only surfaces the transactional events after the commit control message is written (contrasted against the Confluent Cloud Console UI, which uses read_uncommitted and shows messages immediately). Activity 2 is a browser-based Gitpod lab (no local install required) that has the reader inspect consumer-group describe output, specifically the CURRENT-OFFSET and LOG-END-OFFSET columns, to see that the next-read position equals the next-write position when caught up; produce a message with a specific key and observe which partition it lands on to demonstrate key-based routing; and read the LAG column to understand how many produced-but-unconsumed messages sit on a partition. It also has the reader stop/restart consumers and observe consumer-group behavior, though it does not walk through rebalancing mechanics explicitly. Confirmed live and working when fetched, both activities have concrete steps and cleanup instructions.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: acks controls producer durability with a latency/durability tradeoff
description: The producer configuration docs describe three acks levels: 0 (fire-and-forget, no server ack), 1 (wait for the leader broker's ack only -- can lose data if the leader fails before followers replicate), and all (wait for acknowledgment from every in-sync replica, the strongest durability guarantee Kafka offers at the producer level). The current documented default is 'all'. The docs state a hard constraint, not just a recommendation: 'enabling idempotence requires this config value to be all' -- so a producer that wants exactly-once-style deduplication cannot trade away durability by lowering acks. This is presented as a genuine choice for producers not using idempotence: acks=1 is faster but can silently lose the most recent unreplicated write on leader failure; acks=all is slower but survives leader failure as long as one in-sync replica is alive.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: At-least-once still requires an idempotent consumer, even with careful commit ordering
description: The standard at-least-once recipe is enable.auto.commit=false plus a manual commit issued only after the consumer has fully processed a batch's side effects. This closes the message-loss failure mode of auto-commit (never marking a message done before it's actually done) but does not and cannot close the duplicate-processing failure mode: if the process crashes or is rebalanced away after the side effect (e.g. a DB write or downstream publish) succeeds but before the offset commit is acknowledged, the next owner of that partition will start from the last committed offset and reprocess the already-applied message. This is why every at-least-once consumer that has externally visible side effects needs its own idempotency mechanism (dedup key, upsert semantics, idempotent API call) independent of anything Kafka's client does -- the guarantee Kafka gives is about redelivery, not about effects. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://tarkalabs.com/blogs/kafka-message-duplication/ describes duplicates arising from a poll-timeout eviction and rebalance ('Kafka will assume that the service is dead... the same message will then be assigned to, and processed by, another consumer in the group'), not from 'a crash between finishing processing and committing the offset' as the row asserts. The conclusion (at-least-once needs an idempotent consumer) is right and the article does present that solution; the stated mechanism is not the cited one.]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Choosing commitSync vs commitAsync is a throughput/safety tradeoff, not a correctness switch
description: commitSync() blocks the polling thread until the broker acknowledges the commit, and it will automatically retry on retriable errors -- this is reliable but forces the consumer loop to pay a network round-trip and reduces throughput. commitAsync() does not block and optionally takes a callback for success/failure, which is faster under load, but a failed async commit is not automatically retried by the client, and because commits can be reordered, blindly retrying a stale async commit risk overwriting a later, valid commit with an older offset. The judgment call practitioners have to make deliberately: use commitAsync() in the steady-state poll loop for throughput, but call commitSync() on rebalance (in the revoke callback) and on shutdown, where a blocking guarantee actually matters and there's no 'next commit' to fall back on.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Cooperative/incremental rebalancing replaces stop-the-world eager rebalancing
description: The original eager protocol forces every consumer to revoke all of its partitions at the start of every rebalance, even the ones it will be reassigned right back afterward, causing avoidable processing downtime. KIP-429's cooperative approach lets consumers retain currently-owned partitions through the rebalance's join phase; a partition is only revoked, via a follow-up rebalance, if its ownership is genuinely changing. This 'minimizes partition movement' when paired with a sticky assignor. The KIP names the CooperativeStickyAssignor as the built-in implementation and adds an onPartitionsLost() callback distinguishing voluntary revocation from forced ejection from the group. The KIP is explicit about the tradeoff: cooperative rebalancing 'is really expecting the plug-in assignor to be sticky' -- with a non-sticky assignor it merely adds extra rebalance rounds without reducing cost, and the upgrade path itself requires two rolling bounces of the fleet instead of one.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Decoupling consumption from processing via a worker thread pool
description: The javadoc's recommended pattern for handling slow or variable-latency processing: 'move message processing to another thread, which allows the consumer to continue calling poll while the processor is still working,' combined with disabling automatic commits and manually committing 'processed offsets for records only after the thread has finished handling them.' This is presented as a choice among two documented multi-threading patterns -- one-consumer-per-thread (simplest, 'often the fastest', but uses more TCP connections) versus decoupled consumption/processing (a single consumer feeding a thread pool via a blocking queue, which 'allows independently scaling the number of consumers and processors' but requires careful coordination so offsets are only committed for fully-processed records).

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: enable.auto.commit and its data-loss risk
description: enable.auto.commit defaults to true, with auto.commit.interval.ms defaulting to 5000ms, meaning offsets are committed roughly every 5 seconds regardless of processing progress. The javadoc warns explicitly: 'if you fail to [consume all data before subsequent calls or closing], it is possible for the committed offset to get ahead of the consumed position, which results in missing records' -- i.e. records can be silently skipped on the next restart if the consumer crashes after an auto-commit but before finishing processing of the corresponding batch. This is a judgment call the docs surface directly: auto-commit is simple and adequate when occasional message loss on crash is acceptable, but manual commit is required when correctness demands at-least-once processing.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: End-to-end exactly-once requires a specific combination of producer and consumer settings together
description: The Kafka design documentation is explicit that 'achieving exactly-once requires: transactional producer with transactional.id set, plus consumer using isolation.level=read_committed and enable.auto.commit=false. This ensures atomicity across both production and offset tracking.' This is a judgment-level configuration decision because each piece is individually necessary but not sufficient: enabling idempotence alone only deduplicates a single producer's retries; enabling transactions alone without read_committed lets a downstream consumer see uncommitted (possibly-aborted) data; and auto-commit racing against transactional writes can commit consumer offsets independently of whether the corresponding output write actually committed, breaking the atomicity the whole scheme exists to provide.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: fetch.min.bytes trades latency for throughput/efficiency
description: Documented as 'the minimum amount of data the server should return for a fetch request,' with a default of 1 byte -- meaning by default the broker returns data as soon as any is available, prioritizing low latency. Raising fetch.min.bytes (paired with fetch.max.wait.ms as the latency cap) causes the broker to wait for more data to accumulate before responding, which reduces the number of fetch round-trips and request overhead per byte transferred, at the direct cost of added end-to-end latency for low-throughput partitions. This is a standard throughput-vs-latency dial the docs present as a tunable rather than a fixed correctness setting.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: max.poll.interval.ms and the processing-time / liveness tradeoff
description: If poll() is not called again within max.poll.interval.ms, the javadoc states 'the client will proactively leave the group so that another consumer can take over its partitions,' which can surface to the application as a CommitFailedException on the next commit attempt. The docs explicitly name the failure mode: a consumer that keeps sending heartbeats (so it looks alive) but never calls poll() again because it is stuck processing is a 'livelock.' This makes max.poll.interval.ms a judgment call tied to worst-case processing latency per poll() batch, not a fixed operational constant -- setting it too low causes spurious rebalances under normal load spikes, too high delays detection of a truly stuck consumer.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: max.poll.records bounds work-per-poll but not time-per-poll
description: Documented as 'the maximum number of records returned in a single call to poll(),' defaulting to 500. This setting only bounds batch size, not wall-clock time: 500 records that each take 100ms to process would still take 50 seconds of processing, which could exceed max.poll.interval.ms if that is left at its default of 300000ms (5 min) or lower. The two settings are commonly confused because they both relate to the poll loop, but they answer different questions -- max.poll.records answers 'how much work can one poll() hand me,' max.poll.interval.ms answers 'how long do I have to finish that work before the group considers me dead.' Tuning one without the other is a common source of the livelock/rebalance failure mode described in the max.poll.interval.ms row.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: session.timeout.ms / heartbeat.interval.ms is a failure-detection-speed vs false-eviction tradeoff
description: session.timeout.ms (broker-side default 45s at the time reviewed) is how long the group coordinator waits without a heartbeat before declaring a member dead and triggering a rebalance; heartbeat.interval.ms (default 3s) is how often the client sends heartbeats, and is recommended at no more than 1/3 of session.timeout.ms so a few missed heartbeats don't immediately trip eviction. This is a judgment call, not a fixed-answer setting: a shorter session.timeout.ms detects genuinely crashed consumers faster (less downstream lag before another member takes over their partitions), but it also raises false-positive evictions during normal but momentarily slow behavior -- a GC pause, a slow disk flush, a brief CPU spike -- which then trigger a full rebalance for a consumer that was never actually dead. A related documented failure mode is a rebalance that never stabilizes: Kafka bug KAFKA-2985 records a consumer group that, after a load-test-induced session-timeout wave, kept re-forming with a new generation number over and over (generations 16 through 24+) rather than settling, with members hitting UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID and being unable to commit -- the ticket was closed as 'Not A Problem,' i.e. treated as expected behavior of the protocol under sustained heartbeat loss rather than a bug to fix, which is itself the trap: practitioners expect a rebalance storm to self-heal quickly and it is not guaranteed to. Description also calls session.timeout.ms a 'broker-side default'; under the classic protocol it is a consumer client config. topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Static membership (group.instance.id) trades faster restarts for slower failure detection
description: KIP-345 introduces group.instance.id as a stable, user-provided identifier that survives process restarts, replacing the ephemeral member.id normally regenerated on each join. When a static member restarts within the session timeout, the broker returns its cached assignment immediately with no group-wide rebalance -- this targets two use cases the KIP names directly: heavy stateful applications where rebalancing causes major performance degradation, and rolling deployments where each instance bounce would otherwise trigger a rebalance. The KIP is explicit about the cost: this design is 'prioritizing state persistence over liveness,' meaning a truly failed static member is not detected until session.timeout.ms expires rather than via an explicit leave-group signal (static members deliberately skip sending LeaveGroup on shutdown). The KIP recommends extending session timeouts to as much as 30 minutes for this pattern, and warns that duplicate group.instance.id values across consumers cause a FENCED_INSTANCE_ID error.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: transactional.id enables cross-session recovery and zombie-producer fencing
description: The producer-configs docs describe transactional.id as enabling 'reliability semantics which span multiple producer sessions since it allows the client to guarantee that transactions using the same TransactionalId have been completed prior to starting any new transactions.' KIP-98 frames the underlying design tradeoff: a stable transactional.id lets the coordinator recognize when a new producer instance is restarting with the same identity as a previous one and needs to resolve that previous instance's dangling transaction before proceeding -- and it lets the coordinator bump an internal epoch to fence off ('zombie') the old instance if both are somehow still running, so an old, stale producer process cannot write into a transaction a newer instance has already taken over. This is a judgment call for operators: transactional.id must be assigned per logical producer identity (e.g. per partition-owning task), not shared across concurrently-running instances, or fencing will reject legitimate writers.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: auto.offset.reset triggers surprise replay or silent data skip
description: auto.offset.reset controls what a consumer does when it has no committed offset for a partition or the committed offset is out of range -- but people configure it once at setup and forget it can activate later, unexpectedly, e.g. when offsets.retention.minutes expires an old committed offset for a low-traffic consumer group, or a consumer group is inadvertently treated as new. The two settings then fail in opposite, equally dangerous directions: 'earliest' can replay millions of historical messages the consumer never intended to reprocess, while 'latest' silently skips everything already in the log, permanently losing any messages produced between the last real commit and the reset event. Neither is a 'safe default' -- the choice has to be a deliberate decision tied to how the consumer's downstream side effects behave under replay versus loss.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Idempotent producer scope
description: The idempotent producer assigns each producer instance a unique Producer ID (PID) plus a per-partition monotonically increasing sequence number; the broker only accepts a write whose sequence number is exactly one greater than the last accepted one for that (PID, partition) pair, which rejects duplicate retries. The trap: this state is scoped to a single producer session and a single partition. If the producer application restarts, it is issued a new PID and sequence numbers reset to zero -- so duplicates are possible across restarts even with idempotence enabled. It also does nothing about duplicates already present in the data the producer read from its own source (e.g. a duplicate read from an upstream system); Kafka cannot deduplicate what the producer already sent it twice.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: RangeAssignor can produce lopsided assignment across multiple topics
description: RangeAssignor lays out each topic's partitions in numeric order and the group's consumers in lexicographic order, then divides partition count by consumer count per topic -- consumers early in that ordering get any remainder partitions. Because this is done independently per topic rather than globally, a consumer subscribed to multiple topics can end up with a disproportionately large share of total partitions: the documented example is 2 topics x 4 partitions with 3 consumers, where consumer 1 gets 4 partitions (one extra from each topic) while consumers 2 and 3 get 2 each. This is a decision people get wrong by assuming 'range' means an even split -- it only guarantees an even split within a single topic, and the imbalance compounds with topic count. Kafka's default assignment strategy since 2.4+ is CooperativeStickyAssignor, which does not have this per-topic stacking behavior, but RangeAssignor remains available and is still explicitly configured in some codebases.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Scope of exactly-once semantics
description: The most common EOS misconception is treating it as an end-to-end guarantee: 'we're using Kafka with exactly-once semantics, so we don't have to worry about duplicates.' In reality Kafka's exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions) only guarantees that writes to Kafka topics/partitions and Kafka Streams state are applied once. The moment a consumer does anything outside Kafka -- writes to a database, calls a REST API, publishes to another queue -- that write is outside the transaction boundary. If the consumer crashes after the external write but before committing its offset, the record is reprocessed on restart regardless of EOS being enabled upstream. The article's recommended defenses are idempotent consumer logic, the transactional outbox pattern, and offset-aware idempotency keys, not relying on Kafka EOS alone.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Cooperative rebalancing internals: owned-partitions field and consecutive-rebalance-as-barrier
description: Mechanistically, KIP-429 changes what information flows through the group protocol: subscriptions now carry an 'owned partitions' field so the assignor knows what each member currently holds, not just what it wants. Rather than a single global synchronization point where every member must revoke before anyone gets a new assignment, the protocol uses consecutive rebalances as the synchronization mechanism -- a member holding a partition that is moving keeps it through the first rebalance round, then revokes it (triggering a second, smaller rebalance) once the target owner is known. Listener callbacks only fire for partitions that actually changed, not for the full assignment on every rebalance, which is a behavioral change from the eager protocol's listener semantics.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Group coordinator, generation ID, and the JoinGroup/SyncGroup/Heartbeat/LeaveGroup RPCs (classic protocol)
description: The Kafka protocol guide states 'each group in the cluster is assigned to one of the brokers (its group coordinator) to facilitate group management.' On a rebalance, 'when new members join an existing group, all previous members are required to rejoin by sending a new join group request'; the coordinator then 'select[s] one member to be the group leader and a protocol which is supported by all members.' Critically, assignment computation itself happens on the client, not the broker, in this classic protocol: 'the sync group request is used by the group leader to assign state (e.g. partition assignments) to all members of the current generation... only the leader provides the group's assignment.' The coordinator increments a generation ID on every rebalance and rejects stale-generation requests, forcing lagging members to rejoin. Heartbeat requests keep a member's session alive; if none arrive within session.timeout.ms 'the member will be kicked out of the group.' LeaveGroup exists because it 'is preferred over letting the session timeout expire since it allows the group to rebalance faster' -- an explicit exit is detected immediately, whereas silence is only detected after the full timeout window.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Idempotent producer: producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers
description: KIP-98 introduces the mechanism behind enable.idempotence: each producer session gets a unique PID transparently at initialization. For every (PID, TopicPartition) pair the producer maintains a sequence number starting at zero and incrementing by one per message. The broker validates that an incoming message's sequence number is exactly one greater than the last one it committed for that (PID, partition); a duplicate (already-seen) sequence number is silently deduplicated, while a gap (a sequence number skipping ahead) is treated as a fatal error signaling data loss. This is what converts producer-retry-driven duplication -- previously an unavoidable side effect of at-least-once retries -- into effectively-exactly-once writes for a single producer session, without requiring the application to dedupe anything itself.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Next-generation consumer group protocol moves assignment computation server-side
description: KIP-848's stated motivation is operational: 'we have had many bugs in the rebalance protocol over the last years and the majority of them required client side bug fixes,' and in managed/cloud environments fixing a protocol bug 'depend[s] on the adoption of the clients.' The classic protocol's global synchronization barrier means 'a single misbehaving consumer can take down or disturb the whole group because a rebalance of the whole group is required whenever a consumer joins, leaves or fails.' The new protocol makes assignment declarative and server-driven: 'the assignor defines the desired state for the group and let the group coordinator converge to it,' so members reconcile toward their target assignment independently and a partial group update (one member's assignment changing) no longer requires a full-group rebalance. Enabling it requires setting group.protocol=consumer on the client; once active, several classic-protocol consumer configs (heartbeat.interval.ms, session.timeout.ms, partition.assignment.strategy) are no longer used -- their broker-side equivalents (group.consumer.*) apply instead. Stated tradeoffs: client-side custom assignors are not supported under the new protocol, and Kafka Connect does not support it as of the source reviewed. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Summary asserts '(default from Kafka 4.0, group.protocol=consumer)'. KIP-848 itself states: 'In the beginning, the new protocol will be disabled by default. We envision enabling it by default in a future major release of Kafka.' The Kafka 4.3 consumer-configs page gives group.protocol Default: classic. The parenthetical is contradicted by its own cited source, by row K-010, and by this row's own description ('Enabling it requires setting group.protocol=consumer on the client').]

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Original design: automatic consumer load balancing as the precursor to the modern group coordinator
description: The original design deck (Kreps, Narkhede, Rao; hosted on the Apache Kafka project wiki) shows 'Auto Consumer Load Balancing' as: brokers and consumers register in ZooKeeper, consumers listen to broker and consumer registration changes, and each such change triggers a consumer rebalance. This is architecturally distinct from the current protocol (a dedicated broker-side group coordinator driving JoinGroup/SyncGroup/Heartbeat, later evolving further under KIP-848 into fully server-computed assignment) but establishes the enduring shape of the problem the modern protocol still solves: partition ownership must be recomputed and redistributed whenever group membership changes, and every generation of the protocol is an answer to how to do that recomputation with minimal disruption. Coverage of the ZooKeeper-to-KRaft transition itself is out of scope for this harvest; this row only establishes the historical shape of the rebalance problem.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Original design: stateless broker, consumer-held position, retention-driven deletion
description: The original Kafka design presentation by its creators (Kreps, Narkhede, Rao at LinkedIn), archived as an official attachment on the Apache Kafka project wiki, states the principle as 'Efficiency #3: Stateless Broker' -- 'each consumer maintains its own state' and 'message deletion driven by retention policy, not by tracking consumption,' which the authors call 'acceptable in practice' and note enables a 'rewindable consumer.' This is a foundational architectural decision that explains why Kafka retains messages for a fixed window regardless of consumption (unlike a traditional queue that deletes on ack): the broker's job is to be a dumb, efficient append-only log, and all consumption bookkeeping is pushed to the client side. It directly explains why consumer position being 'just a single integer' (separate row) is possible at all -- the broker has no competing notion of per-message state to reconcile it against.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Transaction coordinator, transaction log, and commit/abort markers
description: KIP-98 describes the three components that make multi-partition atomicity possible: applications need 'the ability to write to several TopicPartitions atomically... either all messages are committed, or none of them are.' Each transactional producer connects to a transaction coordinator, a broker role that assigns PIDs, tracks transaction state, and drives commit/abort. The transaction log is an internal Kafka topic that durably persists this metadata so in-flight transactions can be recovered after a coordinator failure. When the producer calls commitTransaction() or abortTransaction(), the coordinator writes a COMMIT or ABORT marker as a control message to every partition that participated in the transaction; consumers use these markers to decide whether to surface or discard the transactional messages that preceded them.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Assemble the minimum config set for end-to-end exactly-once
description: List the settings without notes. Then, for each, answer what specifically breaks if it is left at its default. A setting you cannot break-justify is one you have memorized rather than understood.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Classify a pipeline's real delivery guarantee end to end
description: Sketch a pipeline that reads from Kafka, transforms, and writes to an external database. Annotate each hop with its true guarantee. The point of the drill is arriving at the boundary where Kafka's exactly-once claim stops applying and your own idempotency has to take over. Repeat with transactions enabled and see which hop changes.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Predict rebalance behavior before running it
description: Pick concrete numbers (for example 3 consumers, 8 partitions). Predict the assignment under RangeAssignor and under CooperativeStickyAssignor. Then predict what changes when a fourth consumer joins, when one is SIGKILLed, and when one blocks for longer than max.poll.interval.ms. Check the last case against what the coordinator actually does, since it differs from the first two.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Re-derive why a poison pill stalls one partition and not the topic
description: Reason from the single-integer-offset model rather than from a remembered answer. Then list the exits (skip, dead-letter topic, retry with backoff) and name the guarantee each one costs you.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Trace the loss and duplicate windows for each commit strategy
description: Write out a three-column table: auto-commit, sync-commit-after-process, sync-commit-before-process. For each, mark the instant a crash produces loss and the instant it produces a duplicate. The exercise is done when you can state which strategy gives at-most-once and which gives at-least-once without looking it up, and can point at the line of code where the window opens.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Consumer lag: CURRENT-OFFSET versus LOG-END-OFFSET
description: Confluent's Kafka Technical Fundamentals lab defines lag as 'how many messages have been written to the current partition but have not yet been consumed', and walks through reading it from the consumer-group listing where 'the LOG-END-OFFSET shows the offset to which the next message would be written' against the group's CURRENT-OFFSET. Lag is the operational counterpart to everything the offset rows describe: a group that is committing correctly but processing too slowly looks healthy by every other signal and is only visible as growing lag, and because lag is per partition, a single hot or stalled partition (see the poison-pill trap, K-020) shows as one partition's lag climbing while the group's other partitions read zero. It is also the measurement that makes the max.poll.interval.ms tradeoff (K-036, K-038) concrete rather than theoretical. Added by audit: lag appears in this run only inside exercise K-026, so a reader who does not run the lab never encounters it -- an operational must-know reachable only by doing.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Partition count is the ceiling on group parallelism, and ordering is per-partition
description: Two consequences of the one-partition-to-one-consumer rule that the row set states nowhere, both in canon the run already opened. On parallelism, the KafkaConsumer javadoc says of the one-consumer-per-thread model: 'The number of total threads across all processes will be limited by the total number of partitions.' A group with more members than the topic has partitions leaves the extras assigned nothing; scaling a consumer group past the partition count buys zero throughput, and the only remedy is adding partitions (which is itself not free -- the 4.3 consumer-configs page warns that 'altering partition numbers while setting this config to latest may cause message delivery loss'). On ordering, the design page says the topic 'is divided into a set of totally ordered partitions, each of which is consumed by exactly one consumer within each subscribing consumer group at any given time' -- total order holds inside a partition and nowhere else, so any cross-partition sequencing a reader assumes is unfounded, and the message key (which selects the partition) is what actually buys ordering for a given entity. Added by audit: K-004 states the exclusivity rule but neither of these consequences, and both are load-bearing for reading K-014, K-043 and K-054 correctly.

topic: Kafka consumer mechanics and delivery semantics
subject: Position vs committed position, and the n+1 commit rule
description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc is explicit that 'there are actually two notions of position relevant to the user of the consumer: The position of the consumer gives the offset of the next record that will be given out. It will be one larger than the highest offset the consumer has seen in that partition... The committed position is the last offset that has been stored securely. Should the process fail and restart, this is the offset that the consumer will recover to.' It then states the rule that manual-commit code gets wrong: 'Note: The committed offset should always be the offset of the next message that your application will read. Thus, when calling commitSync(offsets) you should use nextRecordToBeProcessed.offset() or if ConsumerRecords is exhausted already ConsumerRecords.nextOffsets() instead.' Committing record.offset() rather than record.offset()+1 does not fail loudly -- it silently reprocesses exactly one record per commit, forever, which is invisible in any test that tolerates at-least-once. The same section adds a second correction to the naive mental model: 'offsets are not guaranteed to be consecutive (such as compacted topic or when records have been produced using transactions)', so code that infers message loss from a gap in offsets is wrong. Added by audit: K-002 establishes that position is a single integer at orientation depth and K-006 covers commitSync vs commitAsync, but no row in the set states what value to commit.
